claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, growth ceases in response to a peak of the molting hormone ecdysone that coincides with a nutrition-dependent checkpoint, critical weight.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, growth ceases in response to a peak of the molting hormone ecdysone that coincides with a nutrition-dependent checkpoint, critical weight.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work throughout the manuscript.

claim: Insulin/insulin-like growth factor signaling (IIS)/Target of Rapamycin (TOR) signaling in the prothoracic glands (PGs) regulates ecdysone biosynthesis and critical weight.
source: Previous studies indicate that insulin/insulin-like growth factor signaling (IIS)/Target of Rapamycin (TOR) signaling in the prothoracic glands (PGs) regulates ecdysone biosynthesis and critical weight.
evidence: This claim is attributed to previous studies and is cited in the abstract.

claim: FoxO directly interacts with Ultraspiracle (Usp), part of the ecdysone receptor.
source: We show that Forkhead Box class O (FoxO), a negative regulator of IIS/TOR, directly interacts with Ultraspiracle (Usp), part of the ecdysone receptor.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through GST-pulldown and co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpressing FoxO in the PGs delays ecdysone biosynthesis and critical weight.
source: While overexpressing FoxO in the PGs delays ecdysone biosynthesis and critical weight, disrupting FoxO–Usp binding reduces these delays.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data shown in Figures 3, 4, 6, and 7.

claim: Disrupting FoxO–Usp binding reduces the delays in ecdysone biosynthesis and critical weight caused by FoxO overexpression.
source: While overexpressing FoxO in the PGs delays ecdysone biosynthesis and critical weight, disrupting FoxO–Usp binding reduces these delays.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with FoxO NK mutant shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Feeding ecdysone to larvae eliminates the effects of critical weight.
source: Further, feeding ecdysone to larvae eliminates the effects of critical weight.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1B and Figure 6C-D.

claim: Nutrition controls ecdysone biosynthesis partially via FoxO–Usp prior to critical weight.
source: Thus, nutrition controls ecdysone biosynthesis partially via FoxO–Usp prior to critical weight, ensuring that growth only stops once larvae have achieved a target nutritional status.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The small ecdysone peak that occurs around 10 hr after L3 ecdysis in well-fed larvae is suppressed in starved larvae until at least 18 hr after L3 ecdysis.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, we found that the small ecdysone peak that occurs around 10 hr after L3 ecdysis (AL3E) in well-fed larvae is suppressed in starved larvae, at least until 18 hr AL3E (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ecdysone measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Wild type larvae reached critical weight at 8.66 hr after L3 ecdysis.
source: Wild type larvae reached critical weight at 8.66 hr AL3E (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1), correlating with the time when well-fed, wild type larvae show a peak of ecdysone (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is determined through breakpoint analysis shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: When 20E was added to the medium, even the youngest larvae no longer delayed their onset of metamorphosis when starved.
source: When we added the active form of ecdysone, 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), to the medium even the youngest larvae no longer delayed their onset of metamorphosis when starved (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1B.

claim: Larvae fed 20E-supplemented fly medium throughout the L3 were more than 25% smaller than control larvae.
source: Finally, larvae fed 20E-supplemented fly medium throughout the L3 were more than 25% smaller than control larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FoxO was localized primarily in the nuclei of the PG cells of newly ecdysed L3 larvae (0 hr AL3E).
source: We found that FoxO was localized primarily in the nuclei of the PG cells of newly ecdysed L3 larvae (0 hr AL3E) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining shown in Figure 2A.

claim: As larvae fed, FoxO was gradually transported out of the nuclei into the cytoplasm.
source: As the larvae fed, FoxO was gradually transported out of the nuclei into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining at different time points shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: By 10 hr AL3E, immediately after critical weight, FoxO was mostly localized in cytoplasm of fed larvae.
source: By 10 hr AL3E, immediately after critical weight (Figure 1B), FoxO was mostly localized in cytoplasm of fed larvae (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: In larvae starved from 0–15 hr AL3E, FoxO remained in the nuclei of the PG cells.
source: In larvae starved from 0–15 hr AL3E, FoxO remained in the nuclei of the PG cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FoxO bound to Usp but not to EcR in vitro.
source: Using GST-pulldown assays, we found that FoxO bound to Usp but not to EcR in vitro (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GST-pulldown assays shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FoxO bound to Usp only in pre-critical weight or starved larvae, but not in well-fed post-critical weight larvae.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments using larval extracts showed that FoxO bound to Usp only in pre-critical weight or starved larvae, but not in well-fed post-critical weight larvae (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: FoxO neither bound to EcR, nor did it impede EcR/Usp binding in starved larvae.
source: FoxO neither bound to EcR, nor did it impede EcR/Usp binding in starved larvae (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: The presence of 20E neither changed the binding properties of the FoxO–Usp interaction nor induced a FoxO–EcR association.
source: The presence of 20E neither changed the binding properties of the FoxO–Usp interaction nor induced a FoxO–EcR association (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GST-pulldown assays with 20E shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Larvae overexpressing FoxO in the PGs using Phm-Gal4 attained critical weight at larger sizes and 10 hr later than controls.
source: We used Phantom (Phm)-Gal4, a Gal4 driver specific for the PG cells, to overexpress FoxO in the PGs. These larvae attained critical weight at larger sizes and 10 hr later than in controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through critical weight analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Overexpressing Usp in the PGs did not produce any significant difference in either the size or the age at which critical weight was achieved.
source: Overexpressing Usp in the PGs did not produce any significant difference in either the size or the age at which critical weight was achieved (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through critical weight analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Overexpressing both FoxO and Usp in the PGs resulted in larvae that reached critical weight more than 13 hr later and about 1 mg larger than control larvae.
source: Overexpressing both FoxO and Usp in the PGs resulted in larvae that reached critical weight more than 13 hr later and about 1 mg larger than control larvae (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through critical weight analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The size of larvae at critical weight when both FoxO and Usp were overexpressed in the PGs was significantly larger than when either FoxO or Usp was overexpressed in the PGs alone.
source: Further, the size of these larvae at critical weight was significantly larger than when either FoxO or Usp was overexpressed in the PGs alone (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of critical weights shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knocking down either FoxO or Usp alone in the PGs reduced the size but not the age at critical weight.
source: In contrast, knocking down either FoxO or Usp alone in the PGs reduced the size but not the age at critical weight (Figure 3E or Figure 3F, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated through critical weight analysis shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: When both FoxO and Usp were simultaneously knocked down in the PGs, larvae reached critical weight significantly earlier at smaller sizes than knocking down either FoxO or Usp alone.
source: When we simultaneously knocked down both FoxO and Usp in the PGs, larvae reached critical weight significantly earlier at smaller sizes (Figure 3G) than knocking down either FoxO or Usp alone (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through critical weight analysis shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Overexpressing either FoxO or Usp in the PGs significantly increased body size compared to parental controls.
source: Overexpressing either FoxO or Usp in the PGs significantly increased body size compared to parental controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharate adult weight measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Females that overexpressed both FoxO and Usp together in the PGs had significantly larger body sizes than those overexpressing either FoxO or Usp alone.
source: In addition, females that overexpressed both FoxO and Usp together in the PGs had significantly larger body sizes than those overexpressing either FoxO or Usp alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, ANOVA interaction term, p = 0.045).
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharate adult weight measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knocking down Usp resulted in a significant decrease in body size.
source: Knocking down Usp resulted in a significant decrease in body size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharate adult weight measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knocking down both Usp and FoxO in the PGs dramatically reduced body size.
source: However, knocking down both Usp and FoxO in the PGs dramatically reduced body size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharate adult weight measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: In parental controls, both phm and dib increased in expression around 8 hr AL3E, shortly before the critical weight ecdysone peak.
source: In the parental controls, both phm and dib increased in expression around 8 hr AL3E, shortly before the critical weight ecdysone peak (Figure 4A,B,D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 4A, B, D, E.

claim: E74B expression peaks around 12 hr in parental controls, after the critical weight ecdysone peak.
source: E74B expression peaks around 12 hr in parental controls, after the critical weight ecdysone peak (Figure 4C,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 4C, F.

claim: When both FoxO and Usp were overexpressed in the PGs, the increase in phm and dib expression was delayed.
source: When both FoxO and Usp were overexpressed in the PGs, the increase in phm and dib expression was delayed (Figure 4A,B) and e74B expression remained low up to 20 hr AL3E (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: When FoxO and Usp were knocked down, both phm and dib expression levels were high immediately after the molt to the L3.
source: In contrast, when we knocked down FoxO and Usp, both phm and dib expression levels were high immediately after the molt to the L3 (Figure 4D,E) and e74B expression was nearly undetectable at ecdysis but increased rapidly thereafter (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The Usp binding site in FoxO was narrowed down to a 35 amino acid region overlapping with 5 amino acids in the C-terminal end of the forkhead (DNA binding) domain.
source: We created overlapping GST-tagged FoxO fragments and, using increasingly smaller overlapping fragments, we narrowed down the Usp binding region to a 35 amino acid region overlapping with 5 amino acids in the C-terminal end of the forkhead (DNA binding) domain (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GST-pulldown assays with FoxO fragments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Usp binding motif in FoxO is well conserved across arthropod species including ticks and water fleas, but is not conserved in FoxO proteins in other ecdysozoans or vertebrates.
source: This motif is well conserved across arthropod species including ticks and water fleas, but is not conserved in FoxO proteins in other ecdysozoans or vertebrates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At least 4 of the 18 amino acid residues tested (W172, N175, R202 and K204) appeared to be involved in FoxO–Usp binding.
source: At least 4 of the 18 amino acid residues appeared to be involved in FoxO–Usp binding (residues W172, N175, R202 and K204).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutagenesis and GST-pulldown assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Four double–mutant combinations (W172-R202, W172-K204, N175-R202, and N175-K204) were sufficient to dramatically reduce FoxO–Usp interactions.
source: We then tested four double–mutant combinations (W172-R202, W172-K204, N175-R202, and N175-K204) all of which were sufficient to dramatically reduce FoxO–Usp interactions (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GST-pulldown assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Two double–mutant combinations (N175-R202 or FoxO NR, and N175-K204 or FoxO NK) showed normal translocation to the nucleus and did not affect FoxO's ability to regulate InR and 4E-BP promoter activities.
source: The remaining two double–mutant combinations (N175-R202 or FoxO NR, and N175-K204 or FoxO NK) showed normal translocation to the nucleus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) and did not affect FoxO's ability to regulate InR and 4E-BP promoter activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunocytochemistry and luciferase assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Overexpression of FoxO and FoxO NK reduced organ size to a similar degree when driven in wings and eyes.
source: For all drivers, overexpression of FoxO and FoxO NK reduced organ size to a similar degree (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through organ size measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Larvae that overexpressed FoxO NK in their PGs reached critical weight earlier and at smaller sizes than those that overexpressed wild type FoxO, albeit later than the parental controls.
source: Larvae that overexpressed FoxO NK in their PGs reached critical weight earlier and at smaller sizes than those that overexpressed wild type FoxO, albeit later than the parental controls (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through critical weight analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pupae in which FoxO NK was overexpressed in the PGs were significantly smaller than pupae that overexpressed wild type FoxO, although they were still larger than pupae from the parental controls.
source: Similarly, pupae in which FoxO NK was overexpressed in the PGs were significantly smaller than pupae that overexpressed wild type FoxO, although they were still larger than pupae from the parental controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through pupal weight measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpressing FoxO in the oenocytes and corpora allata does not affect the duration of the L3.
source: We found that overexpressing FoxO in the oenocytes and corpora allata does not affect the duration of the L3. In contrast, overexpressing FoxO in the ring glands using P0206-Gal4 prolonged the duration of the L3 compared to parental controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through L3 duration measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Overexpressing FoxO in the oenocytes and corpora allata did not affect final body size, whereas overexpressing FoxO using P0206-Gal4 increased body size.
source: Further, overexpressing FoxO in the oenocytes and corpora allata did not affect final body size, whereas overexpressing FoxO using P0206-Gal4 increased body size (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through body size measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FoxO null larvae that overexpressed FoxO NK in their PGs reached critical weight earlier and at smaller sizes than larvae that overexpressed wild type FoxO in their PGs.
source: Similar to what we found in the FoxO wild type background, FoxO null larvae that overexpressed FoxO NK in their PGs reached critical weight earlier and at smaller sizes than larvae that overexpressed wild type FoxO in their PGs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through critical weight analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Overexpressing both FoxO NK and Usp in the PGs of FoxO null mutant larvae did not alter the age and size at critical weight compared to overexpressing FoxO NK alone.
source: Further, we confirmed that overexpressing both FoxO NK and Usp in the PGs of FoxO null mutant larvae did not alter the age and size at critical weight (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) nor did it alter final body size when compared to overexpressing FoxO NK alone (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through critical weight and body size measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: In parental controls, larvae starved before 12 hr AL3E on ecdysone-supplemented agar did not delay the onset of metamorphosis, pupariating 36 hr after starvation.
source: In the parental controls, larvae starved before 12 hr AL3E on ecdysone-supplemented agar did not delay the onset of metamorphosis, pupariating 36 hr after starvation (Figure 6C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through starvation experiments with 20E shown in Figure 6C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 20E administration eliminated the strong delays in time to metamorphosis seen in pre-critical weight P0206>FoxO, FoxO null larvae.
source: This suggests that (1) 20E administration eliminated the strong delays in time to metamorphosis seen in pre-critical weight P0206>FoxO, FoxO null larvae and (2) FoxO overexpression in the PGs has additional stage-specific effects on the time to pupariation after the critical weight ecdysone peak and this effect is nutrition-sensitive.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both P0206>FoxO, FoxO null and P0206, FoxO null parental control animals were significantly smaller when they were continuously fed 20E-supplemented normal fly medium when compared to animals reared on normal fly medium alone.
source: In addition to the effects we observed on developmental time, we found that both P0206>FoxO, FoxO null and P0206, FoxO null parental control animals were significantly smaller when they were continuously fed 20E-supplemented normal fly medium when compared to animals reared on normal fly medium alone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through body size measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The expression of both phm and dib mRNA peaked shortly before critical weight in the parental controls.
source: The expression of both phm and dib mRNA peaked shortly before critical weight in the parental controls (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 7A-B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: P0206>FoxO, FoxO null larvae showed significant delays in the peak of phm and dib expression.
source: However, P0206>FoxO, FoxO null larvae showed significant delays in this peak (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 7B, D.

claim: Overexpressing FoxO NK in the PGs reduced the delays in phm and dib expression induced by FoxO overexpression.
source: Overexpressing FoxO NK in the PGs reduced the delays induced by FoxO overexpression (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 7B, D.

claim: In the parental control larvae, e74B mRNA expression was up-regulated around 12 hr AL3E, shortly after critical weight.
source: In the parental control larvae, e74B mRNA expression was up-regulated around 12 hr AL3E, shortly after critical weight (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpressing FoxO in the PGs delayed the up-regulation of e74B in both the FoxO mutant and wild type backgrounds.
source: Overexpressing FoxO in the PGs delayed the up-regulation of e74B in both the FoxO mutant and wild type backgrounds (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Interfering with FoxO/Usp complexes, by overexpressing FoxO NK, in the PGs reduced the delay in e74B expression in both the FoxO mutant and wild type backgrounds.
source: Finally, interfering with FoxO/Usp complexes, by overexpressing FoxO NK, in the PGs reduced this delay in both the FoxO mutant and wild type backgrounds (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpressing FoxO in the PGs of FoxO mutant larvae induced a significant delay in the critical weight ecdysone peak.
source: Overexpressing FoxO in the PGs of FoxO mutant larvae induced a significant delay in the critical weight ecdysone peak (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ecdysone measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The maximum concentration of the critical weight ecdysone peak in P0206>FoxO larvae was approximately 50% lower than the critical weight ecdysone peak in parental controls.
source: In addition, the maximum concentration of this peak was approximately 50% lower than the critical weight ecdysone peak in parental controls.
evidence: This is inferred from the ecdysone measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The critical weight ecdysone peak occurred significantly earlier in P0206>FoxO NK larvae than in P0206>FoxO larvae.
source: The critical weight ecdysone peak occurred significantly earlier in P0206>FoxO NK larvae than in P0206>FoxO larvae.
evidence: This is inferred from the ecdysone measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Overexpressing either FoxO or FoxO NK induced indistinguishable reductions in PG size.
source: Overexpressing either FoxO or FoxO NK induced indistinguishable reductions in PG size (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PG size measurements shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Environmental conditions influence developmental processes by affecting hormone synthesis in many organisms.
source: Environmental conditions influence developmental processes by affecting hormone synthesis in many organisms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by general knowledge in the field.

claim: Increasing IIS/TOR activity in the PGs induces precocious critical weight and reducing its activity in the PGs prolongs this transition.
source: Increasing IIS/TOR activity in the PGs induces precocious critical weight and reducing its activity in the PGs prolongs this transition (Caldwell et al., 2005; Colombani et al., 2005; Mirth et al., 2005; Layalle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IIS/TOR signaling positively regulates the expression of CYP450 ecdysone biosynthetic genes, phm and dib.
source: Because IIS/TOR signaling positively regulates the expression of CYP450 ecdysone biosynthetic genes, phm and dib (Colombani et al., 2005; Layalle et al., 2008), we previously hypothesized that IIS/TOR exerted these effects by regulating the timing of the small peak of ecdysone that coincides with critical weight (Mirth and Riddiford, 2007; Mirth and Shingleton, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During the molt to the L3, larvae undergo a period of starvation while they expel their mouthparts.
source: During the molt to the L3, larvae undergo a period of starvation while they expel their mouthparts (Park et al., 2002, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For other ecdysone peaks, a negative feedback loop induced by ecdysone signaling itself down-regulates ecdysone biosynthesis.
source: For other ecdysone peaks, a negative feedback loop induced by ecdysone signaling itself down-regulates ecdysone biosynthesis (Sakurai and Williams, 1989; Takaki and Sakurai, 2003; Moeller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PTTH regulates all ecdysone peaks.
source: Thus in contrast to IIS/TOR signaling whose major effects are to control the critical weight ecdysone peak, PTTH regulates all ecdysone peaks.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is inferred from the cited literature.

claim: Starvation causes a delay in development before attaining critical weight.
source: Even though starvation causes a delay in development before attaining critical weight, once they reach critical weight, starvation induces moderate acceleration in the time to metamorphosis (Mirth et al., 2005; Stieper et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Once larvae reach critical weight, starvation induces moderate acceleration in the time to metamorphosis.
source: Even though starvation causes a delay in development before attaining critical weight, once they reach critical weight, starvation induces moderate acceleration in the time to metamorphosis (Mirth et al., 2005; Stieper et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In other insects, traits such as seasonal wing morphs in butterflies or horn length in male dung beetles arise from differential regulation of ecdysone biosynthesis.
source: In other insects, traits such as seasonal wing morphs in butterflies (Koch and Bückmann, 1987; Koch et al., 1996; Oostra et al., 2011) or horn length in male dung beetles (Emlen and Nijhout, 1999) arise from differential regulation of ecdysone biosynthesis (Koyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Horn length in dung beetles is highly nutrition-dependent, with small, poorly-fed males bearing small horns and large, well-fed males having disproportionately larger horns.
source: Horn length in dung beetles is highly nutrition-dependent, with small, poorly-fed males bearing small horns and large, well-fed males having disproportionately larger horns (Emlen, 1994, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Small-horned male dung beetles have a characteristic peak of ecdysone in their final instar absent in their well-fed, larger conspecifics.
source: Small-horned males have a characteristic peak of ecdysone in their final instar absent in their well-fed, larger conspecifics (Emlen and Nijhout, 1999, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: FoxO is known to form complexes with many vertebrate NHRs, including thyroid hormone, androgen and estrogen receptors.
source: FoxO is also known to form complexes with many vertebrate NHRs, including thyroid hormone (Zhao et al., 2001), androgen (Li et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2007) and estrogen receptors (Schuur et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In girls, reaching a body mass of 48 kg determines the timing of first menses.
source: In girls, reaching a body mass of 48 kg determines the timing of first menses (Frisch and Revelle, 1970; Freedman et al., 2003; Gluckman and Hanson, 2006; Ahmed et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Obese girls reach 48 kg body mass faster, resulting in earlier onset of puberty.
source: Obese girls reach this mass faster, resulting in earlier onset of puberty (Freedman et al., 2003; Gluckman and Hanson, 2006; Ahmed et al., 2009) possibly due to higher levels of insulin signaling (Codner and Cassorla, 2009; Lee et al., 2011; Lombardo et al., 2009; von Berghes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Two mammalian NHRs, CAR and PXR, associate with FoxO1 to regulate the expression of the CYP450 enzymes.
source: Furthermore, two mammalian NHRs, CAR and PXR, associate with FoxO1 to regulate the expression of the CYP450 enzymes (Kodama et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Usp binding motif in FoxO is different from the well-known 'LXXLL'-type NHR binding motif identified in vertebrates.
source: Interestingly, this Usp binding motif is different from the well-known 'LXXLL'-type NHR binding motif identified in vertebrates (Heery et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Before larvae reach critical weight, starvation delays the onset of metamorphosis.
source: A hallmark of critical weight is that before it is attained starvation delays the onset of metamorphosis (Beadle et al., 1938; Nijhout and Williams, 1974b; Mirth et al., 2005; Shingleton et al., 2005; Stieper et al., 2008), whereas after critical weight larvae metamorphose early when starved.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: After critical weight, larvae metamorphose early when starved.
source: A hallmark of critical weight is that before it is attained starvation delays the onset of metamorphosis (Beadle et al., 1938; Nijhout and Williams, 1974b; Mirth et al., 2005; Shingleton et al., 2005; Stieper et al., 2008), whereas after critical weight larvae metamorphose early when starved.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Feeding ecdysone to larvae with genetically-induced delays in critical weight rescues the timing of the onset of metamorphosis.
source: Feeding ecdysone to larvae with genetically-induced delays in critical weight rescues the timing of the onset of metamorphosis (Stieper et al., 2008; Parker and Shingleton, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The IIS/TOR pathway controls body size by regulating growth rate, and also by regulating the timing of critical weight to determine the duration of the growth period.
source: The IIS/TOR pathway controls body size by regulating growth rate, and also by regulating the timing of critical weight to determine the duration of the growth period (Nijhout, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: At critical weight, the IIS/TOR pathway acts directly on the prothoracic glands (PGs) to alter the timing of the expression of several cytochrome P450 (CYP450) genes necessary for ecdysone biosynthesis.
source: At critical weight, the IIS/TOR pathway acts directly on the glands that synthesize ecdysone, the prothoracic glands (PGs), to alter the timing of the expression of several cytochrome P450 (CYP450) genes necessary for ecdysone biosynthesis (Colombani et al., 2005; Layalle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Under well-fed conditions, insulin-like peptides (ILPs) are secreted into the insect blood or hemolymph.
source: Under well-fed conditions, insulin-like peptides (ILPs) are secreted into the insect blood or hemolymph (Masumura et al., 2000; Ikeya et al., 2002; Rulifson et al., 2002; Geminard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: By binding to the Insulin Receptor (InR), ILPs activate IIS/TOR signaling in the target tissues.
source: By binding to the Insulin Receptor (InR), ILPs activate IIS/TOR signaling in the target tissues (Brogiolo et al., 2001; Ikeya et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activating IIS/TOR signaling regulates a series of phosphokinases, including Akt.
source: Activating IIS/TOR signaling regulates a series of phosphokinases, including Akt.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is based on established knowledge.

claim: Akt phosphorylates FoxO, displacing it from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: Akt, in turn, phosphorylates a negative regulator of growth, Forkhead Box class O transcription factor (FoxO), displacing it from the nucleus to the cytoplasm (Junger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In starved larvae, FoxO localizes in the nucleus where it acts on its targets, such as 4E-binding protein (4E-BP, also known as Thor), to suppress cell growth and division.
source: In starved larvae, FoxO localizes in the nucleus where it acts on its targets, such as 4E-binding protein (4E-BP, also known as Thor), to suppress cell growth and division (Puig et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In mammalian cells, FoxO binds to several nuclear hormone receptors (NHRs), such as constitutive androstane receptor (CAR) and pregnane X receptor (PXR), to regulate CYP450 expression.
source: In mammalian cells, FoxO binds to several nuclear hormone receptors (NHRs), such as constitutive androstane receptor (CAR) and pregnane X receptor (PXR), to regulate CYP450 expression (Kodama et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The functional ecdysone receptor is composed of two NHRs, Ecdysone Receptor (EcR) and Ultraspiracle (Usp).
source: The functional ecdysone receptor is composed of two NHRs, Ecdysone Receptor (EcR) and Ultraspiracle (Usp).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is based on established knowledge.

claim: Many CYP450 enzymes are involved in ecdysone biosynthesis.
source: Since many CYP450 enzymes are involved in ecdysone biosynthesis (Gilbert et al., 2002), this led us to the hypothesis that the effect of IIS/TOR signaling on ecdysone biosynthesis is mediated by the interaction between FoxO and either EcR or Usp.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A small peak of the steroid hormone ecdysone early in the third larval instar has been proposed to induce critical weight.
source: Early in the third (final) larval instar (L3), a small peak of the steroid hormone ecdysone has been proposed to induce a developmental transition known as critical weight (Mirth and Riddiford, 2007; Mirth and Shingleton, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Environmental cues including nutrition, temperature and oxygen levels affect the timing of the critical weight ecdysone peak.
source: Environmental cues including nutrition, temperature and oxygen levels affect the timing of the critical weight ecdysone peak (Caldwell et al., 2005; Colombani et al., 2005; Mirth et al., 2005; Callier et al., 2013; Ghosh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The neuropeptide prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH) stimulates ecdysone biosynthesis at critical weight.
source: In addition, the neuropeptide important for inducing all ecdysone peaks, prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH), stimulates ecdysone biosynthesis at critical weight (McBrayer et al., 2007; Ou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Critical weight determines the duration of the growth period, and therefore final body size, in response to environmental conditions including nutrition.
source: Critical weight itself determines the duration of the growth period, and therefore final body size, in response to environmental conditions including nutrition (Beadle et al., 1938; Nijhout and Williams, 1974b; Mirth et al., 2005; Shingleton et al., 2005; Stieper et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ablating the PTTH-producing cells delays critical weight.
source: Activating downstream targets of PTTH signaling in the PGs accelerates the onset of metamorphosis (Caldwell et al., 2005) and ablating the PTTH-producing cells delays critical weight (McBrayer et al., 2007; Rewitz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Without PTTH the ecdysone peak that stimulates wandering behavior is dramatically delayed.
source: Further, without PTTH the ecdysone peak that stimulates wandering behavior, where the larvae emerge from the food to begin metamorphosis, is dramatically delayed (McBrayer et al., 2007; Rewitz et al., 2009; Gibbens et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous work.
